beats.narration_text: Vanakkam. This is Liam, in for Bear, with chapter three of INFO 7375, Computational Skepticism for AI, at Northeastern. This film is about blank cells. The reason a value is missing decides whether filling it in is safe. Sort the rows by what you can see, and some blanks line up. Some never will. The trap: the worst kind of missing looks exactly like the harmless kind.

show.event: 'TL;DR.' wordmark; 'Vanakkam, Liam'; the course line; heading

props.heading: What This Film Is About
props.question: Two columns are each 18% blank. Why is one safe to fill in and the other a trap?
lines: The reason a value is missing decides whether filling it in is safe.
Sort the rows by what you can see: some blanks line up. Some never will.
The trap: the worst kind of missing looks exactly like the harmless kind.

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Every dataset you inherit has blanks, and the first fix anyone reaches for is the average. When the reason is harmless, the average lands on the truth. When the people who left it blank are different, it drifts in a direction you cannot measure. Knowing the three kinds tells you which question no plot can answer for you.

beats.narration_text: Three words you'll hear. A missingness matrix: every row a thin line, every column a stripe, dark where a value is absent. Impute: fill a blank with an estimate, such as the average of the values you can see. And a subgroup: rows that share a trait, such as everyone under twenty-five.

fill a blank with an estimate, such as the average of the values you can see

learn.question: Two columns, both 18% blank: which is safe to fill with the average?
learn.action: Draw both missingness matrices in file order.
learn.observation: The blanks look equally scattered in both.
learn.inference: Nothing on screen yet separates them.
learn.next_question: What does an average fill do when the blanks carry no reason at all?

beats.narration_text: Two tables of the same fifty people. In each, the income column is eighteen percent blank: nine rows out of fifty. Look at the dark cells. Scattered, in both. Same count, same look. Fill both with the average income you can see. One fill lands on the truth. The other lands somewhere else. Which is which?

shot.visual_intent: Two missingness matrices, 'table A' and 'table B', draw row by row (stripes: age · city · income; 50 thin rows); nine dark cells scattered in each income stripe; '9 of 50 blank · 18%' under each; the question 'fill with the average: which is safe?' at right; a small dim caption 'constructed table'.

show.event: matrix A draws row by row
nine dark cells land in each income stripe

shot.motion_claim: The key case, unsolved: two matrices with the same 18% that look the same.

learn.question: What does a mean fill do when blanks are pure chance?
learn.action: Fill two different random wipes with the visible average and compare to the known truth.
learn.observation: Both fills land on the truth.
learn.inference: Random loss costs rows, not direction.
learn.next_question: What if the blanks are not random?

beats.narration_text: Start with the easy case: a third table, where nine income cells were wiped at random, a coin flip, nothing to do with the person. Fill the nine with the average of the forty-one you can see. We built this table, so we can reveal the true average. The fill lands right on it. Wipe a different nine at random: it lands on it again. Random loss shrinks your sample. It does not tilt it.

shot.visual_intent: Matrix 'random' at left, nine scattered dark cells; at right an income axis (no numbers, 'lower' / 'higher'); the nine blanks fill grey (imputed) and a fill dot slides onto the axis; the ink 'truth' tick rises under it; then the dark cells move to a second random nine, the fill re-runs and the dot lands on the tick again.

show.event: blanks fill grey; fill dot slides onto the axis
truth tick revealed under the dot
the blanks move to a new random nine
the dot lands on the truth again

shot.motion_claim: The first instance, varied and replayed: random blanks, fill on target.

learn.question: Does the same fill work on table A?
learn.action: Fill A's blanks with the visible average; read the age stripe beside them.
learn.observation: The fill lands high; every blank is under 25.
learn.inference: Blanks tied to a visible column tilt the average.
learn.next_question: Can we fix it with the column we can see?

beats.narration_text: Now table A. Same fill, same average of the visible rows. This time the dot lands to the right of the truth. Too high. Something about who is blank pulled it. Look along the age stripe, beside each dark cell: every blank row belongs to someone under twenty-five. In this table the young earn less, and they are the ones who skipped the question.

shot.visual_intent: Matrix A at left with the age stripe shaded: under-25 rows grey; the nine income blanks fill; the fill dot lands right of the truth tick ('too high'); the under-25 age cells darken, a terracotta dot beside the age header.

show.event: blanks fill; dot lands right of the truth
the age cells beside the blanks darken: all under 25

shot.motion_claim: The second instance: the same fill, a tilted result, and a visible column that correlates with the blanks.

learn.question: Does filling by age group fix both tables?
learn.action: Run the age-group fill on A, then on B.
learn.observation: A lands on the truth; B stays low.
learn.inference: B's blanks are not explained by age — or by anything on screen.
learn.next_question: How could we SEE what the blanks depend on?

beats.narration_text: The natural fix: fill each blank with the average of its own age group. Do it for table A, and the dot slides back onto the truth. Now do exactly the same thing for table B, whose blanks look just as scattered. The dot barely moves. It stays low. And nothing in the table tells you why.

shot.visual_intent: Matrix A with its dot high: the age-group fill runs and the dot slides back onto A's truth tick. Matrix B slides in beside it with its own axis: the column fill, then the age-group fill — the dot stays well left of B's truth tick; a terracotta X beside B's dot.

show.event: A: age-group fill; dot slides onto the truth
B: same fill; dot stays low

shot.motion_claim: The natural wrong turn: the fix that works for A fails for B, with no visible reason.

learn.question: What do the blanks depend on?
learn.action: Re-sort each matrix's rows by each visible column.
learn.observation: A's blanks form a block under age; B's never do.
learn.inference: Sorting by a column tests whether missingness depends on it.
learn.next_question: B depends on nothing visible — so what does it depend on?

beats.narration_text: Here's the move. Stop reading the matrix in file order. Sort the rows by a column you can see, and watch where the blanks go. Sort table A by age: the nine dark cells slide together, all inside the under-twenty-fives. Sort table B by age: still scattered. By city: scattered. A block means the blanks depend on something you can see.

shot.visual_intent: Matrices A and B side by side; A's rows glide into age order and its nine blanks gather in the top band (under 25, bracketed); B's rows glide into age order — blanks stay scattered — then into city order — scattered; caption: a block = depends on a visible column.

show.event: A sorts by age: blanks gather in the under-25 band

shot.motion_claim: The representation: sort rows by a column and watch whether the blanks line up.

learn.question: If we could sort by the value itself, where would B's blanks go?
learn.action: Add the never-recorded true-income bars; hold.
learn.inference: A prediction makes the sort evidence.

beats.narration_text: Table B stays scattered under every column it has. So here is the one column it doesn't have: each person's true income, the value that was never written down. Before I sort by it, commit. Where will table B's nine blanks go? And the random table's?

shot.visual_intent: Matrix B (city order) and the random matrix; a ghost stripe of horizontal bars grows beside each — 'true income, never recorded' — bar length per row; everything holds; 'commit' with a terracotta dot; caption: true income, never recorded.

show.event: the unrecorded true-income bars grow beside both matrices

shot.motion_claim: The predict-before-reveal beat: the hidden column arrives, unsorted.

learn.question: Where do B's blanks go under the hidden sort?
learn.action: Sort both matrices by the true, never-recorded income.
learn.observation: B's blanks are the top nine; the random table's stay scattered.
learn.inference: B's missingness depends on the missing value itself — invisible from inside the data.

beats.narration_text: Sort. Table B's blanks slide into one block at the very top: the nine highest earners. The random table's stay scattered. From inside the data, those two looked identical.

shot.visual_intent: Both matrices re-sort by the true-income bars (bars form a descending staircase): B's nine dark cells glide into one block at the top beside the longest bars; the random table's stay scattered; a terracotta dot beside B's block; 'B: the top nine' · 'random: scattered'.

show.event: both sort by the hidden bars
B's blanks: one block at the top
caption: from inside, they looked the same

shot.motion_claim: The aha: the blanks line up only under the column the matrix cannot draw; narration short.

learn.question: What are these three behaviours called?
learn.action: Name each matrix by what its blanks depend on.
learn.observation: Nothing · something visible · the value itself.
learn.inference: The kind of missingness, not the amount, decides whether a fill is safe.
learn.next_question: If no sort can show MNAR, how does anyone find it?

beats.narration_text: These deserve names, and they come from Donald Rubin's work on missing data. Missing completely at random: the chance of a blank depends on nothing. Missing at random: it depends on something you can see, like age. Missing not at random: it depends on the missing value itself. The first two, a sort can show you. The third, no sort you can run ever will.

shot.visual_intent: The three matrices shrink into one row (random · A · B) in their revealing sorts; under each its name lands (MCAR · MAR · MNAR) with one line: depends on nothing · on what you can see · on the missing value itself; B's hidden bars fade to ghost; a terracotta dot beside MNAR; small dim credit: after Rubin (1976).

show.event: three matrices slide into one row
MAR — on what you can see
MNAR — on the value itself; its bars fade

shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as the name for three things watched; each label beside the matrix that earned it.

learn.question: How do you find MNAR if no plot shows it?
learn.action: Relabel the matrix as a study with dropouts; sort by recorded vs unrecorded columns.
learn.observation: Only the unrecorded sort lines the blanks up.
learn.inference: MNAR is found by reasoning about who would not report, not by a diagnostic.
learn.next_question: Back to tables A and B.

beats.narration_text: Same shape, different table. A study's final measurement, blank for the patients who left before the end. Sort by anything recorded: scattered. The sort that would line them up is who got sicker, which is the very thing that's missing. So you don't find this kind with a plot. You find it by asking: who would not report this, and why?

shot.visual_intent: Matrix B's stripes relabel (visit 1 · visit 2 · final); it sorts by visit 1 — scattered; a ghost stripe 'got sicker, never recorded' grows and the rows sort into a block again; the question 'who would not report this, and why?' lands at right with a terracotta dot; small dim caption: constructed.

show.event: stripes relabel: a study's final measurement
sorted by a recorded column: scattered
the unrecorded 'got sicker' sort: one block

shot.motion_claim: Post-shift instance: the same invariant in a new table; the detector is a question, not a plot.

learn.question: So — which fill is safe?
learn.action: Sort both hook tables by age and fill within the group.
learn.observation: A lands on the truth; B stays low.
learn.inference: Safe depends on why, not how much.

beats.narration_text: Back to the two tables. Both eighteen percent blank, both scattered in file order. Sort by age: table A lines up, so fill within the age group and you land on the truth. Table B never lines up, and its average sits low, biased in exactly the direction you cannot measure. Not taught here: how to choose an imputation method, or rows a join dropped before any matrix could see them.

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK's two matrices return in file order; both sort by age: A gathers, B stays scattered; A's dot on its truth tick, B's dot low with an X beside it; labels MAR / MNAR under each; dim boundary caption: not taught here: choosing a fill.

show.event: A: dot on truth · B: dot low, X

shot.motion_claim: The HOOK's objects resolve; the boundary names what was left out.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Missing is not one thing. If the blanks depend on nothing, an average fill lands on the truth. If they depend on something you can see, like age, sort by it, fill within the group, and you recover it. If they depend on the missing value itself, every fill drifts, and no plot can show you. For that kind, ask who would not report, and why.

artifactLines: Same 18% blank, different reasons — the reason decides whether a fill is safe.
Blanks that depend on nothing (MCAR): an average fill lands on the truth.
Blanks that depend on a column you can see (MAR): sort by it, fill within the group.
Blanks that depend on the value itself (MNAR): no plot shows it. Ask who would not report, and why.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: A clinic dataset has a column pain_score that is 18% blank, and the missingness matrix shows the blanks cluster in evening appointments. Before writing any code, predict: MCAR, MAR, or MNAR? Then give me one story under which it really is MAR, and one under which it is actually MNAR. For each story, say which way an average fill would move the mean pain score, and name one question I should ask the clinic that no plot of this data could answer. Two things to look for. Did it commit to a prediction before it reached for code? And does its MNAR story name who would not report, and why, instead of recommending a fancier fill?
